prompt.adult: Psalm 150 calls for praise with trumpet, lute, harp, timbrel, and cymbals. In its final verse, who or what is called to praise the LORD?
prompt.child: Psalm 150 names lots of instruments for praising God. In the very last verse, who or what should praise the LORD?
prompt.teen: After listing trumpets, harps, and cymbals, Psalm 150 ends by widening the call to praise. Who or what does 150:6 call on?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 150:6, who or what is to praise the LORD?

choices.text: All the trees of the forest

verses.text: Praise Him with the sound of the trumpet; Praise Him with the lute and harp!
Let everything that has breath praise the LORD. Praise the LORD!

explanation.adult: Read the beginning of Psalm 150:6, right after "Let."
explanation.child: Look at the first words of Psalm 150:6. It tells who should praise the LORD.
explanation.teen: 150:3 lists instruments; 150:6 names who should praise. Read the opening of 150:6.
explanation.older: The subject of the final call to praise stands at the start of 150:6.

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 150 is the last psalm, and it is full of praise: in the sanctuary, for God's mighty acts, with trumpet and harp and cymbals. The final verse names who should join in. Read the first words of 150:6.
teaching.takeaway: Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.

prompt.adult: Psalm 122 is a song for worshipers going up to the house of the LORD. In 122:6, what are readers told to pray for?
prompt.child: Psalm 122 is a song about going to worship God together. What does verse 6 tell worshipers to pray for?
prompt.teen: Psalm 122:6 gives a short instruction about prayer. What should be prayed for?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 122:6, for what are readers instructed to pray?

verses.text: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: “May they prosper who love you.

explanation.adult: Read the first line of Psalm 122:6, right after "Pray for."
explanation.child: Look at the start of Psalm 122:6. What to pray for comes right after "Pray for."
explanation.teen: 122:6 begins with an instruction. Read the words after "Pray for."
explanation.older: The object of the prayer follows "Pray for" at the opening of 122:6.

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 122 was sung by worshipers going up to the house of the LORD to give thanks to His name. Verse 6 gives a simple instruction, followed by a blessing. Read the words right after "Pray for."
teaching.takeaway: Psalm 122:6 says to pray for the peace of Jerusalem.

prompt.adult: Psalm 24:3 asks, "Who may ascend into the hill of the LORD?" What two things does 24:4 say that person has?
prompt.child: Psalm 24 asks who may go up to God's holy hill. What two things does the answer say that person has?
prompt.teen: 24:3 asks who may stand in God's holy place, and 24:4 answers. What two things describe that person first?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 24:4, what two qualities belong to the one who may ascend the hill of the LORD?

choices.text: Strong arms and a brave heart
Wise words and a humble spirit
Swift feet and a strong back
Clean hands and a pure heart

verses.text: Who may ascend into the hill of the LORD? Or who may stand in His holy place?
He who has clean hands and a pure heart, Who has not lifted up his soul to an idol, Nor sworn deceitfully.

explanation.adult: Read the first line of Psalm 24:4, right after "He who has."
explanation.child: Look at the start of Psalm 24:4. Two things are named right after "He who has."
explanation.teen: 24:3 asks the question; 24:4 answers it. Read the first pair of things listed.
explanation.older: The opening clause of 24:4 names two qualities of the person; read it closely.

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 24:3 asks who may go up God's hill and stand in His holy place. Verse 4 answers with a description of that person, including what he has not done. Read the first line of 24:4.
teaching.takeaway: The one who may ascend the hill of the LORD has clean hands and a pure heart.

prompt.adult: Psalm 29 praises the power of the voice of the LORD. According to 29:5, what does His voice break?
prompt.child: Psalm 29 says God's voice is powerful and full of majesty. What does it say His voice breaks?
prompt.teen: 29:4 calls the voice of the LORD powerful; 29:5 gives an example. What does it break?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 29:5, what does the voice of the LORD break and splinter?

verses.text: The voice of the LORD is powerful; The voice of the LORD is full of majesty.
The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars, Yes, the LORD splinters the cedars of Lebanon.

explanation.adult: Psalm 29:5 says the same thing twice. Read the end of the verse, after "splinters."
explanation.child: Read Psalm 29:5. Look at the last words, after "splinters."
explanation.teen: 29:5 has two lines that say nearly the same thing. The second line is more specific; read its end.
explanation.older: The second half of 29:5 restates the first more specifically; read what follows "splinters."

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 29 repeats the phrase "the voice of the LORD" again and again, like thunder rolling. Verse 4 says His voice is powerful and full of majesty, and verse 5 gives a picture of that power. Read the end of 29:5.
teaching.takeaway: The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon.

prompt.adult: In Psalm 84:10, the writer says one day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. What humble role would he rather have than dwell in the tents of wickedness?
prompt.child: The writer of Psalm 84 loves being near God so much that he would take a lowly job there. What job?
prompt.teen: 84:10 compares one day in God's courts with a thousand days elsewhere. What role would the writer rather have?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 84:10, what would the psalmist rather be than dwell in the tents of wickedness?

verses.text: For a day in Your courts is better than a thousand. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God Than dwell in the tents of wickedness.

explanation.adult: Read the second line of Psalm 84:10, right after "I would rather be."
explanation.child: Look at Psalm 84:10. The job comes right after "I would rather be."
explanation.teen: 84:10 makes two comparisons. Read the second one, after "I would rather be."
explanation.older: The role is named in the second comparison of 84:10, following "I would rather be."

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 84 is full of longing to be near God: even birds find a nest near His altars (84:3). Verse 10 says one day near Him is better than a thousand elsewhere, and then names a humble role the writer would gladly take. Read the words after "I would rather be."
teaching.takeaway: The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God.

prompt.adult: Psalm 95:6 says, "Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD our Maker." What does 95:7 say we are, as the reason?
prompt.child: Psalm 95 invites everyone to bow down and kneel before God. What does verse 7 say we are?
prompt.teen: 95:6 calls us to kneel; 95:7 begins with "For" and gives the reason. What does it say we are?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 95:7, what does the psalmist say we are, in the reason given for kneeling before Him?

verses.text: Oh come, let us worship and bow down; Let us kneel before the LORD our Maker.
For He is our God, And we are the people of His pasture, And the sheep of His hand. Today, if you will hear His voice:

explanation.adult: Psalm 95:7 gives the reason with "For." Read the words right after "we are."
explanation.child: Read Psalm 95:7. Look right after "we are."
explanation.teen: 95:7 gives two descriptions of us after "we are." Read the first one.
explanation.older: The first description in 95:7 follows "we are."

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 95:6 calls worshipers to bow and kneel before the LORD their Maker. Verse 7 gives the reason, beginning "For He is our God." Read the words right after "we are."
teaching.takeaway: We are the people of His pasture and the sheep of His hand.

prompt.adult: Psalm 19:7 says the law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul. In 19:10, the writer says these words are more desired than gold. What second comparison does he make?
prompt.child: Psalm 19 says God's law is perfect and changes lives. It also says God's words are better than gold. What else does he compare them to?
prompt.teen: 19:7 praises the LORD's law; 19:10 compares it to treasures. Besides being worth more than gold, what is the second comparison?
prompt.older: Connecting Psalm 19:7 with 19:10, after comparing the LORD's law and judgments to gold, what second comparison does the psalmist make?

choices.text: Dates fresh from the palm tree

verses.text: The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul; The testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple;
More to be desired are they than gold, Yea, than much fine gold; Sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.

explanation.adult: Psalm 19:10 makes two comparisons. Read the second one, right after "Sweeter also than."
explanation.child: Read the end of Psalm 19:10, after "Sweeter also than."
explanation.teen: 19:10 compares God's words to something precious and something sweet. Read the second comparison.
explanation.older: The second comparison in 19:10 follows "Sweeter also than"; read it closely.

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 19:7-9 lists the law, testimony, statutes, commandment, and judgments of the LORD and what each one does. Verse 10 then says they are worth more than gold and gives a second comparison about taste. Read the end of 19:10.
teaching.takeaway: The LORD's words are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

prompt.adult: Psalm 8:4 asks, "What is man that You are mindful of him?" In 8:5, the psalmist answers with what God has done for man. With what has God crowned him?
prompt.child: Psalm 8 wonders why God pays attention to human beings at all. Then it says God has crowned man with two things. What are they?
prompt.teen: 8:4 asks why God cares about man; 8:5 answers. What two things has God crowned him with?
prompt.older: Connecting Psalm 8:4 with 8:5, with what does the psalmist say God has crowned man?

verses.text: What is man that You are mindful of him, And the son of man that You visit him?
For You have made him a little lower than the angels, And You have crowned him with glory and honor.

explanation.adult: Read the end of Psalm 8:5, right after "You have crowned him with."
explanation.child: Look at the last words of Psalm 8:5, after "crowned him with."
explanation.teen: 8:4 asks a question; 8:5 answers it with two statements. Read the second one.
explanation.older: The second clause of 8:5 names what God has crowned man with.

teaching.extended_explanation: Psalm 8:4 asks why the God who made the heavens would think about man at all. Verse 5 answers by describing the place God has given man: a little lower than the angels, and crowned with two things. Read the end of 8:5.
teaching.takeaway: God has crowned man with glory and honor.
